title: Building a Portfolio
promise: Single trades are battles. Your portfolio is the war.
unlock: Spread your money so one bad pick only hurts a little
Spot holdings that look different but move together
Split money between stocks, bonds and cash by goal and time
Rebalance a drifting portfolio back to its target
See what a small yearly fee costs over 20 years
Score your results against the right benchmark
Size your portfolio for a fall you can live through

questions.q: You have $20,000: $10,000 in one stock and $1,000 in each of 10 others. The big holding falls 40%. How much do you lose?
options: $4,000: a fifth of all your money
questions.why: Only the big holding fell, but it was half your money. Its 40% fall costs $4,000, a fifth of your $20,000.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: You own one bank stock. Which addition spreads your risk the most?
questions.why: Two banks face the same rates and news, so they tend to fall together. A bond fund is a different asset type.
questions.work: Bank stocks often drop together on the same news. Bonds often move differently, though not always.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: You need $15,000 for a wedding in 18 months. In this example, where does that money belong?
options: Mostly stocks: they grow the most
Cash and short-term bonds: it must be there on the day
Half in one stock, half in cash
questions.why: Money you need within 2 to 3 years stays out of stocks. A crash right before the wedding could leave you short.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: Your target is 70% stocks, 30% bonds. After a bad year you have $6,000 in stocks and $4,000 in bonds. What brings you back to target?
questions.why: Rebalancing tops up what lagged. Stocks are now below target, so move money from bonds into stocks.
questions.work: Total $10,000. 70% = $7,000 in stocks. $7,000 − $6,000 = $1,000 to move from bonds.

questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: Two funds track the same index. Fund A charges 0.05% a year, Fund B 0.75%. On $40,000, how much more does B cost this year?
questions.why: Compare the fees as a gap: 0.75% − 0.05% = 0.70% a year on the same $40,000.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: Your stock portfolio returned 14% after costs. Your benchmark, a broad stock index, returned 18%. Cash paid 4%. How did you do?
options: You lagged your benchmark by 4 points
You beat the index by 4 points
questions.why: Judge a stock portfolio against a stock index, not against cash. The index made more.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: You have $50,000. In a crash, Mix A could fall 40% and Mix B 15%. You know you’d sell in panic after a $10,000 loss. Which mix fits you?
options: Mix A: more growth is worth it
Mix B: a fall you can sit through
questions.why: Mix A’s fall is twice your limit. Pick the fall you can sit through, so you don’t sell at the bottom.

retry.q: You have $50,000 split equally across 20 stocks. One of them goes to zero. How much of your money do you lose?
retry.why: Each stock held a twentieth of your money. Losing all of one costs that slice, and the other 19 are untouched.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: You own 3 airline stocks and 2 cruise-line stocks. Fuel prices jump and people travel less. What likely happens?
options: They mostly fall together: it’s one bet on travel
They cancel out: five different companies
retry.why: Airlines and cruise lines face the same fuel costs and the same travel demand, so the same news hits all five.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: Ana, 30, is saving for retirement at 65. Leo needs his money for school fees in 2 years. In these examples, who can keep more in stocks?
options: Ana: she has decades to recover from falls
Neither: stocks are only for experts
retry.why: Ana has 35 years to sit through falls. Leo’s money must be there in 2 years, so it belongs in cash and bonds.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: Your target is 60% stocks, 40% bonds. After a strong year you have $15,000 in stocks and $5,000 in bonds. What brings you back to target?
options: Sell $3,000 of stocks, buy $3,000 of bonds
retry.why: Stocks grew past target, so trim them and top up bonds until the split is back to 60/40.

retry.q: Two funds track the same index. Fund A charges 0.2% a year, Fund B 1.2%. On $25,000, how much more does B cost this year?
retry.why: Compare the fees as a gap: 1.2% − 0.2% = 1% a year on the same $25,000.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: Your bond portfolio returned 5% after costs. A broad bond index returned 4%. A stock index returned 20%. How did you do?
options: It can’t be compared to anything
You beat your benchmark by 1 point
retry.why: Bonds belong next to a bond index, not a stock index. Against the right bar, you came out ahead.

retry.q: Your portfolio peaked at $60,000, fell to $45,000, and is now at $54,000. What was the drawdown?
retry.why: A drawdown runs from the peak to the low after it, measured against the peak.

refresher.title: Lesson 1 · Don’t put all your eggs in one basket
refresher.text: Spread money so one bad pick hurts a little. A 50% fall in a stock that’s a tenth of your money costs you 5%. Work out each holding’s share first.

refresher.title: Lesson 2 · Correlation: when everything falls together
refresher.text: Assets that move together don’t protect each other. Two banks are one bet. Mix asset types, like stocks and bonds.

refresher.title: Lesson 3 · Asset allocation
refresher.text: The sooner you need the money, the less of it sits in stocks. Money needed within 2–3 years stays in cash and bonds.

refresher.title: Lesson 4 · Rebalancing
refresher.text: Rebalancing brings the split back to target: trim what grew, top up what lagged. Work out the target in dollars from the total first.

refresher.title: Lesson 5 · Costs that compound
refresher.text: Compare fees as a gap: 0.75% − 0.05% = 0.70%. On $40,000 that’s $280 more a year. Fees compound, so check the yearly fee first.

refresher.title: Lesson 6 · Measuring your results
refresher.text: A gain only counts next to the right benchmark: an index that matches what you hold. Compare a stock portfolio with a stock index, not cash.

refresher.title: Lesson 7 · Drawdown: staying in the game
refresher.text: Size for the worst fall you could live through. If a fall would make you sell at the bottom, you hold too much risk.

refresher.title: Lesson 1 · Don’t put all your eggs in one basket
refresher.text: A fall only hits the money in that holding: holding × fall. $2,000 × 50% = $1,000, or 10% of a $10,000 portfolio.

refresher.title: Lesson 2 · Correlation: when everything falls together
refresher.text: Five stocks in one industry face the same news, so they move together. That’s one bet five times, not five bets.

refresher.title: Lesson 4 · Rebalancing
refresher.text: Target % × the whole portfolio = where you should be. The difference from what you hold now is what you move.

refresher.title: Lesson 6 · Measuring your results
refresher.text: Pick a benchmark that matches what you hold: large stocks against a large-stock index, bonds against a bond index.

refresher.title: Lesson 7 · Drawdown: staying in the game
refresher.text: A drawdown is the fall from the peak to the low, measured against the peak: $10,000 ÷ $40,000 = 25%.
